idiom_name: Hash#slice / Hash#except (core Ruby) with as_json(only:) for objects
implementation_notes: Ruby's core Hash carries the projection: payload.slice(:id, :reference) returns a new hash with exactly those keys (keys that are absent stay absent, no exception), and except(:internal_notes) inverts it, so for hash-shaped messages the pattern is one core method call and no filter object exists at all. For objects and richer shapes, ActiveSupport's as_json(only: [...]) / ActiveModel serializers declare the same projection in a class, which is the framework realization of the classic structure. A hand-written recursive filter is still justified for deep trees where the retained fields sit at fixed paths - the flattening case - because slice is shallow and a serializer per shape is often more ceremony than the projection needs.
code_sketch:
PUBLIC_KEYS = %i[id reference total].freeze

def public_view(message)
  message.slice(*PUBLIC_KEYS)   # core Ruby; absent keys stay absent
end

payload = JSON.generate(public_view(JSON.parse(raw, symbolize_names: true)))
pitfalls: Hash#slice is shallow: nested hashes and arrays travel whole, so 'remove the customer's email' needs a nested slice (or a serializer), not one call.
Symbol and string keys are different keys - without symbolize_names: true on parse (or with mixed sources) slice(:id) returns an empty hash and the payload ships empty without an error.
as_json(only:) is ActiveSupport, not core Ruby: outside Rails it is simply absent, and the object then serializes every attribute.
Programs that pass the sliced hash around still share references with the source (slice copies the hash, not the values), so mutating a retained nested object still mutates the original message.
